definition: Fungible means a unit of a good can be freely substituted for another unit of the same commodity. A megawatt of power is not fungible across locations or times in general, but a specific power product (fixed zone, delivery hour, and date) is fungible. Notional value is the face value of a contract (quantity times price), fixed at inception and not necessarily related to the contract's trading profit or risk.
core_idea: Power's physical constraints (can't move it freely across time/location) mean fungibility only holds once a contract is fully specified down to location, hour, and date — this is what makes standardized power contracts tradable at all.
key_points: A share of IBM stock is fungible; any share substitutes for any other.
Raw megawatts of power are not fungible across locations (e.g., New York vs. Los Angeles).
A fully specified power delivery (zone + date + hour) IS fungible, per the author's example.
Notional value example: selling 1,000 barrels of oil at $80 has a notional value of $80,000.
Notional value stays fixed over the contract's life and may have no relationship to actual trading P&L or risk.
relationships: Fungibility is a precondition for standardized exchange trading of a security.
trading_implications: Because power is only fungible once fully specified (location, date, hour), standardized power contracts must be defined at that granularity to be tradable/exchangeable.
caveats: Assuming notional value reflects a contract's actual risk or expected profit — the author explicitly says it may have no relationship to either.

variables.Quantity: contract size, e.g. barrels or MWh
